etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English copy, copie, from Old French copie (“abundance, plenty; transcript, copy”), from Medieval Latin copia (“reproduction, transcript”), from Latin cōpia (“plenty, abundance”), from *coopia, from co- (“together”) + ops (“wealth, riches”). More at opulent.

definitions.definition: The result of copying; an identical duplicate of an original.

quote.citation: 1656, John Denham, preface to The Destruction of Troy:
quote.text: I have not the vanity to think my copy equal to the original.

definitions.definition: An imitation, sometimes of inferior quality.
(journalism) The text that is to be typeset.
(journalism) A gender-neutral abbreviation for copy boy.
(marketing, advertising) The output of copywriters, who are employed to write material which encourages consumers to buy goods or services.
A printed edition of a book or magazine.
Writing paper of a particular size, called also bastard.
(obsolete) That which is to be imitated, transcribed, or reproduced; a pattern, model, or example.

quote.citation: 1669, William Holder, Elements of Speech: An Essay of Inquiry into the Natural Production of Letters: […], London:  […]  T. N[ewcomb] for J[ohn] Martyn printer to the R[oyal] Society, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Let him first learn to write, after a copy of all the letters.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) An abundance or plenty of anything.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), B. I. [i.e., Ben Jonson], The Comicall Satyre of Euery Man out of His Humor. […], London:  […]  [Adam Islip] for William Holme, […], published 1600, →OCLC, Act II, scene i, signature F, verso:
quote.text: [S]he was bleſt with no more Copie of wit, but to ſerue his Humor thus.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: But in them nature's copy's not eterne

definitions.definition: (genetics) The result of gene or chromosomal duplication.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English copien, from Old French copier and Medieval Latin cōpiō.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To produce an object identical to a given object.

quote.citation: 2014 June 21, “Magician’s brain”, in The Economist, volume 411, number 8892:
quote.text: [Isaac Newton] was obsessed with alchemy. He spent hours copying alchemical recipes and trying to replicate them in his laboratory. He believed that the Bible contained numerological codes. The truth is that Newton was very much a product of his time.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To give or transmit a copy to (a person).
(transitive, computing) To place a copy of an object in memory for later use.

quote.citation: 1793, Dugald Stewart, Outlines of Moral Philosophy:
quote.text: We copy instinctively the voices of our companions, their accents, and their modes of pronunciation.
